hook: Same weights, same tokenizer, and one model answers your question while the other writes a fake forum thread. That gap is post-training.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same architecture, same tokenizer. One model answers your question. The other one continues it like a forum post. That gap is post-training.

0:15 QUESTION — Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-0.6B are almost the same weights. Why does one follow instructions and the other ramble? InstructGPT showed a 1.3B tuned model beat 175B GPT-3 in human preference. What changed was not scale.

1:00 INTUITION — Pretraining builds a document simulator. Post-training picks one character out of all the documents it could write: the helpful assistant. Show the InstructGPT three-step pipeline: SFT, reward model, PPO. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Pretraining: maximize sum_t log p(x_t | x_<t) over web text. SFT: same loss, but only on assistant tokens of curated demos. RLHF: maximize E[r(x,y)] - beta * KL(pi || pi_ref). Say why each stage exists: SFT gives format, RM turns preferences into a number, RL optimizes that number without drifting far.

5:00 CODE — Load Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B with AutoModelForCausalLM on the Mac (mps). Write generate(model, tok, prompt, max_new_tokens=128, do_sample=False). Feed both the raw string 'How do I reverse a list in Python?'. Then feed the instruct model the same prompt through tok.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True). Print all three side by side.

8:00 RECEIPT — Score the next-token distribution after the prompt for both models: compute entropy of softmax(logits[-1]). Expected: the instruct model has much lower entropy at the first answer token. Also check the base model gives a coherent answer when you few-shot it with two Q/A examples, proving the knowledge was already there.
10:00 MEASURE — A table of 10 prompts: did the base model answer (yes/no), did the instruct model answer, mean first-token entropy for each. Show the few-shot base row too.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Post-training does not teach facts, it selects a behavior the base model can already produce. Interview line: SFT teaches format, RL teaches preference, and both start from what pretraining already knows.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Chat templates and loss masking
key_math: L_pretrain = -sum_t log p_theta(x_t | x_<t); L_SFT = -sum_{t in assistant} log p_theta(y_t | x, y_<t); J_RLHF = E_{x, y~pi}[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL( pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x) )
code_task: generate(model, tok, prompt, max_new_tokens) -> str for Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-0.6B; first_token_entropy(model, input_ids: [1, T]) -> float from logits[0, -1, :] of shape [V]; a 10-prompt comparison table, plus a 2-shot prompt for the base model.
receipt: Qwen3-0.6B (instruct) first-answer-token entropy < base entropy on at least 8 of 10 prompts; the 2-shot base model produces the correct answer on the list-reversal prompt, matching the instruct model's content.
gotchas: Forgetting apply_chat_template so the instruct model looks as bad as the base; Qwen3 instruct models emit <think> blocks by default, so pass enable_thinking=False in the template or strip them; sampling with temperature makes the comparison noisy, use greedy.
interview_q: What does post-training add if the base model already knows the facts? Model answer: It changes the output distribution to a narrow, useful mode: following instructions, formatting, refusing, and preferring answers humans rate higher. Capability mostly comes from pretraining; post-training elicits and shapes it.
explainer: Here are two boxes labeled base and instruct, holding nearly identical weights, and the same prompt flowing into both of them.
The base model treats the prompt as the start of a web page, so it keeps writing more questions instead of answering.
Pretraining makes a simulator of every kind of document, so the model can play any author it has seen.
Post-training is choosing one author out of that crowd, the careful assistant, and making it the default voice.
InstructGPT did this in three steps on screen now: supervised demos, a reward model from rankings, then reinforcement learning against it.
The result surprised people: a 1.3 billion parameter tuned model was preferred over the 175 billion parameter raw model.
So in this module we build every one of those boxes ourselves, from loss masking to GRPO on math.

hook: If your SFT loss includes the user's tokens, you are training your model to impersonate the user. One mask fixes it.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — If your fine-tuning loss includes the user's words, you are teaching the model to write the user's half too. One mask fixes it.

0:15 QUESTION — Every chat model, Llama 3, Qwen3, Claude, sees conversations as one flat token stream with special role markers. Get the template or the mask wrong and the model leaks roles, never stops, or learns nothing useful.

1:00 INTUITION — A chat is a screenplay flattened into one line. Special tokens are the stage directions. The loss mask is a highlighter: we only grade the lines the assistant speaks. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Cross-entropy with a mask: L = sum_t m_t * CE(logits_t, y_t) / sum_t m_t, where m_t = 1 only on assistant tokens, including the end-of-turn token. PyTorch does this with ignore_index=-100 on labels. Show why the denominator counts only unmasked tokens.

4:30 CODE — Write build_example(messages, tok) -> (input_ids [T], labels [T]). Render with tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False), find each assistant span by tokenizing the prefix up to that turn, set labels = input_ids on assistant spans, -100 elsewhere. Shift happens in the model: labels align with input_ids, HF shifts internally. Print a colored token view: gray masked, green trained.

8:00 RECEIPT — Zero-contribution test: perturb a user token's label (not input) and assert the loss is bitwise unchanged; perturb an assistant token's label and assert it changes. Then compare your mask to TRL: SFTTrainer with assistant-only loss (see TRL docs for the current flag name) on the same example, assert identical masked positions.
10:00 MEASURE — Count trained tokens vs total tokens on a real dataset slice, e.g. 1,000 conversations. Show the fraction, often 30 to 60 percent, which is how much of the loss you would have wasted.
11:00 TAKEAWAY — The mask decides what the model learns to say. Interview line: train on assistant tokens plus the end-of-turn token, or the model never learns to stop.
11:30 NEXT — Next: SFT from scratch
key_math: L = (1 / sum_t m_t) * sum_t m_t * ( -log p_theta(y_t | y_<t) ), m_t = 1 iff token t is in an assistant turn (incl. <|im_end|>)
code_task: build_example(messages: list[dict], tok) -> input_ids LongTensor [T], labels LongTensor [T] with -100 outside assistant spans; masked_ce(logits [B,T,V], labels [B,T]) -> scalar using F.cross_entropy(..., ignore_index=-100) after shifting; a token visualizer that colors masked vs trained tokens.
receipt: Changing labels at a masked (user) position leaves loss identical (torch.equal); changing an assistant label changes it. Masked positions match those produced by TRL's assistant-only-loss path on the same Qwen3 conversation.
gotchas: Tokenizing turns separately and concatenating gives different tokens at the boundaries than tokenizing the full rendered string; forgetting to train on the end-of-turn token so the model never stops; double-shifting labels when the HF model already shifts internally.
interview_q: Why do we mask the prompt during SFT? Model answer: The goal is the conditional p(response | prompt). Including prompt tokens spends capacity modeling user text, biases the model toward producing user-style turns, and dilutes the gradient on the tokens we care about.
explainer: Here is a three-turn chat, system, user and assistant, shown as speech bubbles before we flatten anything.
The template glues them into one stream of tokens, with special markers like im_start and im_end between the roles.
Our model only ever sees this flat stream, so the markers are the only way it knows who is speaking.
Now the highlighter: we color assistant tokens green and everything else gray, and only green tokens enter the loss.
The im_end token after the assistant is green too, because that token is how the model learns to stop talking.
In code, gray means label minus one hundred, which cross entropy skips, and the average divides by green tokens only.
Flip a gray label and the loss does not move at all, which is exactly the receipt we check.

hook: Supervised fine-tuning is the pretraining loop with three changes. We make them, and Qwen3-0.6B-Base starts following instructions in twenty minutes.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — SFT is the pretraining loop with three changes. Make them and Qwen3-0.6B-Base starts following instructions in about twenty minutes on one H100.
0:15 QUESTION — Every open chat model ships an SFT stage first. CS336 Assignment 5 starts here too. What are the three changes, and how do you know your loop is right instead of just lucky?
1:00 INTUITION — Pretraining reads the whole library. SFT is a short course with an answer key: smaller learning rate, masked loss, packed or padded chat examples. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Same masked cross-entropy from last episode. Learning rate about 1e-5 to 2e-5 for full fine-tuning, cosine decay, warmup 3 percent. Tokens per step = batch * seq_len * mask fraction; that number, not examples, controls noise. Mention catastrophic forgetting: small LR and few epochs keep you close to the base.

4:30 CODE — sft_step(model, batch, opt): logits = model(input_ids, attention_mask).logits; loss = masked_ce(logits[:, :-1], labels[:, 1:]); loss.backward(); clip_grad_norm_(1.0); opt.step(). Collate with right padding, pad labels with -100. bf16 autocast, AdamW(lr=2e-5, betas=(0.9,0.95), weight_decay=0.0). Train 1 to 2 epochs on a few thousand examples from a public instruction set. Log loss per trained token.

8:30 RECEIPT — Run TRL SFTTrainer on the same data, same model, same LR, same seed, same batch, and overlay the loss curves. Expected: first-step losses agree to about 1e-3 and the curves track closely. Then a held-out eval: instruction-following on 50 prompts judged by exact format checks.
10:30 MEASURE — Loss curve mine vs TRL, tokens per second, peak memory from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated, and before/after generations on five prompts.
12:00 TAKEAWAY — SFT is small-LR next-token prediction on curated text with a mask. Interview line: SFT is cheap, it sets format and style, and it is the starting point every RL stage depends on.
12:30 NEXT — Next: LoRA from scratch
key_math: L_SFT = -(1/N_mask) sum_{b,t} m_{b,t} log p_theta(y_{b,t} | y_{b,<t}); lr(t) = lr_max * 0.5 * (1 + cos(pi * t / T)) after warmup
code_task: collate(batch) -> input_ids [B,T], attention_mask [B,T], labels [B,T] (-100 on prompt and pad); sft_step(model, batch, opt) -> loss; a training loop with AdamW, cosine schedule, grad clipping 1.0, bf16 autocast on Qwen3-0.6B-Base; evaluate(model, prompts) -> generations.
receipt: Step-0 loss of my loop equals TRL SFTTrainer's step-0 loss on the identical first batch within 1e-3 (same masking, no packing); loss curves overlay within noise over 200 steps.
gotchas: Learning rate copied from pretraining (3e-4) destroys the base model in a few hundred steps; padding tokens without -100 labels pull the model toward predicting pad; Qwen tokenizers have pad_token set to an end token, so masking by pad id can accidentally mask real end-of-turn tokens.
interview_q: Your SFT loss goes down but generations get worse. What do you check? Model answer: Check the mask and template first, then overfitting from too many epochs or too high a learning rate, then data quality. Loss on the training mix says little about held-out behavior, so evaluate generations directly.
explainer: On screen is the pretraining loop we wrote back in module six, with three lines about to change color.
Change one is the data: short chat examples rendered with the template, padded on the right, labels masked.
Change two is the learning rate, roughly ten times smaller, because we want to nudge the model, not rebuild it.
Change three is the length of training, one or two epochs, because more passes start erasing what pretraining learned.
Here is our loss curve in blue and TRL's in orange, starting from the same number and tracking each other.
And here are before and after answers from the same base model, now following the instruction format.
So supervised fine-tuning is not a new algorithm, it is the old loop, aimed carefully.

hook: LoRA trains under one percent of the parameters and often matches full fine-tuning. The trick is two skinny matrices and one zero.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — LoRA trains well under one percent of the weights and often matches full fine-tuning. The whole trick is two skinny matrices and one zero.

0:15 QUESTION — Full fine-tuning a 7B model needs gradients and Adam states for every weight, around 16 bytes per parameter. The LoRA paper cut trainable parameters on GPT-3 175B by 10,000x and GPU memory by about 3x. How?

1:00 INTUITION — The update you need is low rank. Instead of editing a d by k matrix, you add a thin correction: B times A, rank r. Start B at zero so the model is unchanged at step zero. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — h = W0 x + (alpha / r) * B A x, with W0 frozen in R^{d x k}, B in R^{d x r}, A in R^{r x k}, r << min(d,k). Trainable params r(d+k) vs dk; for d=k=4096, r=16 that is 131,072 vs 16.8M, 0.78 percent. Init A ~ Kaiming uniform, B = 0, so Delta W = 0 at start. alpha/r keeps the update scale steady when you change r. Merge: W = W0 + (alpha/r) B A, zero inference overhead.

6:00 CODE — class LoRALinear(nn.Module): __init__(base: nn.Linear, r=16, alpha=32, dropout=0.05); freeze base; self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.empty(r, in_f)); self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(out_f, r)); forward: base(x) + (dropout(x) @ A.T @ B.T) * (alpha / r). merge() returns an nn.Linear with W0 + scale * B @ A. inject_lora(model, targets=['q_proj','k_proj','v_proj','o_proj','gate_proj','up_proj','down_proj']). count_trainable(model).

9:00 RECEIPT — Three asserts. One: at init, LoRA model output equals base output exactly (torch.equal), because B is zero. Two: after a few training steps, merged model output matches unmerged within assert_close(atol=1e-5) in fp32. Three: trainable count matches PEFT: get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules=...)).print_trainable_parameters() reports the same number.
11:00 MEASURE — Table on Qwen3-0.6B: trainable params and percent for r in {4, 16, 64}, attention-only vs all linear layers, and optimizer-state memory saved.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — LoRA is a low-rank, zero-initialized delta you can merge away. Interview line: B starts at zero so training begins exactly at the pretrained model, and alpha over r decouples step size from rank.
12:30 NEXT — Next: QLoRA
key_math: h = W0 x + (alpha/r) B A x; W0 in R^{d x k} frozen, B in R^{d x r} (init 0), A in R^{r x k}; trainable = r(d + k) vs dk; W_merged = W0 + (alpha/r) B A
code_task: LoRALinear(base: nn.Linear, r, alpha, dropout) with A [r, in_features], B [out_features, r]; forward(x [B,T,in]) -> [B,T,out]; merge() -> nn.Linear; inject_lora(model, target_names, r, alpha) replaces matching nn.Linear modules; count_trainable(model) -> int.
receipt: torch.equal(lora_model(x), base_model(x)) at init; torch.testing.assert_close(merged(x), unmerged(x), atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5) after training; my trainable parameter count == PEFT print_trainable_parameters() for the same r and target_modules.
gotchas: Initializing both A and B randomly so the model is perturbed before any training; forgetting to freeze the base weights (requires_grad=False) so the optimizer still allocates full Adam states; merging in bf16 and getting small output drift, merge in fp32 then cast.
interview_q: Why is B initialized to zero in LoRA and not A? Model answer: One of them must be zero so the initial update BA is zero and training starts at the pretrained model. If A were zero, B's gradient would be zero (it depends on Ax), so nothing would train; with B zero, A's output is non-zero and B gets gradient immediately.
explainer: Here is a big frozen weight matrix, four thousand by four thousand, colored gray because we are not allowed to touch it.
Next to it we draw two skinny matrices, B tall and thin, A short and wide, meeting at a rank of sixteen.
Their product is the same shape as the big matrix, but it only has a tiny fraction of the numbers.
We start B at all zeros, so the correction is zero, and the model begins exactly where pretraining left it.
The scale alpha over r sits on the correction like a volume knob, so changing the rank does not change the step size.
After training we add the product into the big matrix once, and inference costs exactly what it did before.
The counter on the right shows the payoff: well under one percent of the parameters actually receive gradients.

hook: QLoRA fine-tuned a 65 billion parameter model on one 48 gigabyte GPU. The base weights sit in 4 bits and never get a gradient.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — QLoRA fine-tuned a 65 billion parameter model on one 48 gigabyte GPU. The frozen weights sit in 4 bits and never get a gradient.

0:15 QUESTION — LoRA cut the optimizer state. But the frozen base still sits in bf16, 2 bytes per weight. For a 7B model that is 14 GB before activations. QLoRA asks: can the frozen part be 4-bit without hurting the fine-tune?

1:00 INTUITION — Store the frozen weights compressed, decompress a layer only when you need it for a matmul, and keep the small LoRA matrices in bf16. NF4 places its 16 levels where normally distributed weights actually live. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — NF4: 16 levels at quantiles of N(0,1), rescaled to [-1,1], with an exact zero. Block-wise absmax with block size 64: w_q = argmin_i |w / absmax_block - level_i|. Scale cost: one fp32 per 64 weights = 0.5 bits per weight. Double quantization: quantize those scales to 8-bit in blocks of 256, cost drops to about 0.127 bits, saving about 0.37 bits per parameter, roughly 3 GB on a 65B model. Paged optimizers: unified memory spills Adam states to CPU during spikes.

6:00 CODE — Build nf4_levels() from torch.distributions.Normal quantiles; quantize_nf4(w, block=64) -> (codes uint8 packed two per byte, absmax [n_blocks]); dequantize_nf4(codes, absmax). Check reconstruction error vs a uniform int4 grid on real Qwen3 weights. Then the real run: BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4', bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16), prepare the model, attach a PEFT LoRA, train 200 SFT steps.

9:00 RECEIPT — Two checks. My dequantize_nf4 reconstruction matches bitsandbytes' dequantized weights for the same tensor (bitsandbytes.functional quantize_4bit and dequantize_4bit with quant_type='nf4'), assert_close within bf16 tolerance. And peak memory: QLoRA run vs bf16 LoRA vs full fine-tune on the 4090, from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated.
11:00 MEASURE — Memory bar chart for Qwen3-1.7B: full FT, LoRA bf16, QLoRA NF4. Plus held-out loss after 200 steps for LoRA vs QLoRA, which should be close.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — QLoRA is LoRA on top of a 4-bit frozen base with a smart codebook. Interview line: gradients flow through the dequantized weights into the adapters, the 4-bit weights themselves are never updated.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Reward models
key_math: NF4 levels q_i = normalized quantiles of N(0,1) (16 levels, exact 0); w_hat = absmax_block * q_{code}; scale overhead = 32/64 = 0.5 bit/param -> with double quant ~ 8/64 + 32/(64*256) ~ 0.127 bit/param
code_task: nf4_levels() -> [16] tensor; quantize_nf4(w [N], block=64) -> codes uint8 [N/2], absmax fp32 [N/64]; dequantize_nf4(codes, absmax) -> [N]; reconstruction MSE vs uniform int4; then a QLoRA SFT run with bitsandbytes 4-bit loading + PEFT LoRA on Qwen3-1.7B.
receipt: assert_close(my_dequantize_nf4(w), bnb dequantize_4bit(quantize_4bit(w, quant_type='nf4', blocksize=64)), atol tied to bf16) on a real weight tensor; QLoRA peak memory well below LoRA-bf16 peak memory on the same model and batch.
gotchas: Using float16 compute dtype and getting overflow, use bf16 compute; forgetting gradient checkpointing so activations, not weights, dominate memory; trying to merge LoRA into the 4-bit weights directly, which re-quantizes and loses quality; dequantize to bf16 first.
interview_q: Why does NF4 beat uniform int4 for LLM weights? Model answer: Pretrained weights are roughly normal, so most values cluster near zero. NF4 puts equal probability mass in each of its 16 bins, so it spends resolution where the weights are, giving lower error at the same bit width.
explainer: This histogram shows real weights from one layer, a bell shape crowded around zero with thin tails.
A uniform four-bit grid puts sixteen evenly spaced levels across it, wasting many of them out in the empty tails.
NF4 instead places sixteen levels at the quantiles of a normal curve, so each bin holds the same share of weights.
Every block of sixty-four weights gets its own absmax scale, and that scale costs half a bit per weight.
Double quantization compresses those scales again to eight bits, bringing the overhead down to about an eighth of a bit.
During the forward pass we decompress one layer, multiply in bf16, and only the small LoRA matrices get gradients.
The memory bars on screen tell the story: the four-bit base shrinks the largest bar by close to four times.

hook: A reward model never sees a score. It only sees pairs, this answer beat that one, and learns a number from that.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A reward model never sees a single score. It only sees pairs, this answer beat that one, and it invents a number that explains them.

0:15 QUESTION — InstructGPT, Llama 2 and most RLHF pipelines train a reward model from human comparisons. Labelers are bad at absolute scores and good at picking a winner. How do you turn winners into a scalar you can optimize?
1:00 INTUITION — Chess Elo. Nobody has a true rating, but wins and losses pin down rating differences. Bradley-Terry is Elo for answers. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Bradley-Terry: P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)). Maximum likelihood gives L = -E log sigma(r_w - r_l). Note only differences matter, so r is defined up to a constant per prompt. Gradient: -(1 - sigma(r_w - r_l)) * (grad r_w - grad r_l), big when the model ranks the pair wrong. InstructGPT normalized rewards so the reference outputs score zero mean.

5:30 CODE — RewardModel(nn.Module): backbone = AutoModel Qwen3-0.6B, head = nn.Linear(d_model, 1, bias=False); forward(input_ids, attention_mask) returns the scalar at the last non-pad token, shape [B]. Batch chosen and rejected together as [2B, T]. Loss = -F.logsigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected).mean(). Train one epoch on a preference dataset such as Anthropic HH-RLHF or UltraFeedback binarized.

9:00 RECEIPT — Held-out pairwise accuracy, mean of (r_chosen > r_rejected). Expected: clearly above 50 percent, and compare to TRL RewardTrainer with the same model and data: its eval accuracy should be within a couple of points of mine. Also assert my per-batch loss equals TRL's loss formula on the same rewards.
11:00 MEASURE — Accuracy vs training steps, the histogram of reward margins r_w - r_l on held-out pairs, and a length check: correlation between reward and response length.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — A reward model is a pairwise classifier whose logit is a reward. Interview line: it only learns reward differences, and it inherits every bias in the labels, including a preference for longer answers.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Policy gradients for LLMs
key_math: P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigma( r_phi(x, y_w) - r_phi(x, y_l) ); L_RM = -E_{(x,y_w,y_l)} [ log sigma( r_phi(x,y_w) - r_phi(x,y_l) ) ]

gotchas: Reading the reward at position -1 when sequences are right-padded, so you score a pad token; chosen and rejected truncated differently so the model learns length instead of quality; leaking the same prompt into train and eval splits.
interview_q: Why train reward models on comparisons instead of scores? Model answer: Humans are inconsistent at absolute ratings but fairly consistent at picking a better answer. Bradley-Terry turns those comparisons into a scalar reward that is identified up to a constant, which is all the policy optimizer needs.
explainer: Here are two answers to the same prompt, with a checkmark on the one the labeler preferred and nothing else.
We pass both through the same transformer, read the hidden state at the last token, and project it to one number.
Now we have two scores, and the only thing the loss cares about is their difference.
The sigmoid of that difference is the probability the winner wins, exactly like an Elo expected score in chess.
When the model ranks the pair backwards, the gradient is large, pushing the winner up and the loser down.
Shift every reward by the same constant and nothing changes, because only differences ever appear in the loss.
Our receipt is simple: on pairs the model never saw, it should pick the human's winner far more than half the time.

hook: Policy gradients are the one idea under PPO, DPO's motivation, and GRPO. Push up the log probability of what scored well.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Under PPO, under GRPO, under every RLHF paper, there is one line: push up the log probability of samples that scored well.

0:15 QUESTION — You cannot backprop through sampling a token or through a reward model's judgment of a finished answer. So how did DeepSeek-R1 and InstructGPT get gradients at all? The log-derivative trick.
1:00 INTUITION — Try things, then do more of what worked. The gradient does not go through the reward, it goes through the probability of the choice you made. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — J(theta) = E_{y~pi_theta}[R(y)]. grad J = sum_y R(y) grad pi(y) = sum_y R(y) pi(y) grad log pi(y) = E[R(y) grad log pi(y)]. For a sequence, log pi(y) = sum_t log pi(y_t | y_<t), so every token of a good answer gets pushed up. Baseline: E[b grad log pi] = b grad sum pi = 0, so subtracting b keeps the gradient unbiased and cuts variance. Advantage A = R - b.

6:00 CODE — Part one, toy bandit: logits = nn.Parameter(zeros(K)); sample a ~ Categorical(logits=logits); loss = -(R(a) - b) * log_prob(a); b is a running mean. Plot learning with and without baseline. Part two, tiny LM: reward = 1 if the sampled 8-token string contains a target word; loss = -(A.detach() * logprobs.sum(-1)).mean() over a batch of samples from a small GPT from M06.

9:00 RECEIPT — Verify the estimator: on a 3-armed bandit, compute the exact gradient of E[R] analytically (softmax Jacobian) and assert the Monte Carlo REINFORCE estimate with 100,000 samples matches within 1 percent. Then show the variance of the estimate with and without baseline: same mean, much smaller variance.
11:00 MEASURE — Reward curve for the bandit with and without baseline over 5 seeds, gradient variance bar chart, and the tiny LM's target-word hit rate rising.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Policy gradient is weighted maximum likelihood on your own samples, weighted by advantage. Interview line: the baseline does not change the expected gradient, only its variance, because the expected score function is zero.
12:30 NEXT — Next: PPO
key_math: grad_theta E_{y~pi_theta}[R(y)] = E_{y~pi_theta}[ R(y) grad_theta log pi_theta(y) ]; E[ b grad log pi_theta(y) ] = 0; g_hat = (1/N) sum_i (R_i - b) sum_t grad log pi_theta(y_{i,t} | y_{i,<t})
code_task: reinforce_bandit(K, R, steps, baseline: bool) -> reward history; exact_grad(logits, R) via softmax Jacobian; reinforce_lm(model, reward_fn, batch=64, len=8): sample with torch.multinomial, gather logprobs [B, L], loss = -(A.detach()[:,None] * logprobs).sum(-1).mean().
receipt: Monte Carlo REINFORCE gradient (1e5 samples) on a 3-armed bandit equals the analytic gradient within 1% (torch.testing.assert_close(rtol=0.01)); baseline version has the same mean and lower empirical variance.
gotchas: Forgetting .detach() on the advantage so gradients flow into the baseline or reward; summing log-probs over padding tokens after the sequence ended; using sampled logits from a no_grad generate call and then trying to backprop through them, recompute logprobs with a grad-enabled forward.
interview_q: Why does subtracting a baseline not bias the policy gradient? Model answer: E_{y~pi}[grad log pi(y)] = grad sum_y pi(y) = grad 1 = 0, so any baseline independent of the sampled action contributes zero in expectation. It only reduces variance.
explainer: Here is a slot machine with three arms and a probability bar over each one, all equal to start.
We pull an arm at random, get a reward, and nudge up the probability of that arm in proportion to how good it was.
The trick in the middle of the screen moves the gradient off the reward and onto the log probability of our choice.
For a sentence, that log probability is a sum over tokens, so every token in a good answer gets a little push.
Without a baseline, every reward is positive, so every arm gets pushed up, and the signal is buried in noise.
Subtract the average reward and only better-than-average choices go up, while the expected gradient stays exactly the same.
The two clouds of gradient estimates on screen share a center, but the baseline cloud is far tighter.

hook: PPO is policy gradient with a seatbelt. One clip function stops a single lucky batch from wrecking your model.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — PPO is policy gradient with a seatbelt. One clip function stops one lucky batch from wrecking the whole model.

0:15 QUESTION — InstructGPT and the original ChatGPT were trained with PPO. Vanilla policy gradient takes one step per batch of expensive samples. PPO reuses each batch for several steps without blowing up. How?
1:00 INTUITION — Importance sampling lets you learn from old samples. The clip says: once the new policy has moved far enough on this token, stop pushing. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Ratio rho_t = pi_theta(a_t|s_t) / pi_old(a_t|s_t). L_clip = E[min(rho_t A_t, clip(rho_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t)], eps = 0.2. Walk through 4 cases: A>0 caps rho at 1+eps; A<0 caps at 1-eps. GAE: delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t), A_t = sum_l (gamma lambda)^l delta_{t+l}. Value loss (V - R_target)^2. RLHF reward per token: r_t = -beta * (log pi - log pi_ref) at each token, plus the RM score at the last token.

6:30 CODE — ppo_policy_loss(logp_new [B,T], logp_old [B,T], adv [B,T], mask [B,T], eps=0.2); value_loss(v [B,T], ret [B,T], mask); gae(rewards [B,T], values [B,T], mask, gamma=1.0, lam=0.95) computed backward in time; kl_penalized_rewards(rm_score [B], logp [B,T], logp_ref [B,T], beta). Whiten advantages over valid tokens.

9:30 RECEIPT — Unit tests. One: when logp_new == logp_old, ppo_policy_loss equals -masked_mean(adv) and its gradient equals the vanilla policy gradient. Two: with A>0 and rho=1.5, gradient is exactly zero (clipped). Three: gae with lam=1, gamma=1 equals reward-to-go minus value. Four: compare against the clipped loss in TRL's PPO implementation or CleanRL on identical tensors, assert_close.
11:30 MEASURE — A plot of the clipped objective vs rho for A=+1 and A=-1, and the clip fraction on a toy run as a diagnostic.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — PPO is trust-region-lite: clip the ratio so reused samples cannot drag the policy too far. Interview line: in LLM RLHF you need four models in memory, policy, reference, reward and value, which is exactly what GRPO later removes.
13:00 NEXT — Next: DPO, derived
key_math: rho_t = pi_theta(a_t|s_t)/pi_old(a_t|s_t); L^CLIP = E_t[ min( rho_t A_t, clip(rho_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t ) ]; delta_t = r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t), A_t = sum_l (gamma lambda)^l delta_{t+l}; r_t = -beta( log pi_theta(y_t|.) - log pi_ref(y_t|.) ) + 1[t=T] r_phi(x,y)
code_task: ppo_policy_loss(logp_new, logp_old, adv, mask, eps) -> scalar; value_loss(values, returns, mask, clip_range=None); gae(rewards [B,T], values [B,T], mask [B,T], gamma, lam) -> advantages [B,T], returns [B,T]; kl_penalized_rewards(rm_score [B], logp [B,T], logp_ref [B,T], mask, beta) -> rewards [B,T]; pytest file with the four tests.
receipt: pytest: loss at rho=1 equals -masked_mean(adv); gradient wrt logp_new is exactly zero where A>0 and rho>1+eps; gae(lam=1,gamma=1) == reward-to-go - values; assert_close against CleanRL/TRL clipped-loss formula on the same random tensors.
gotchas: Computing the ratio from probabilities instead of exp(logp_new - logp_old), which underflows; whitening advantages including padded tokens; letting logp_old carry gradients, it must be detached and computed once before the PPO epochs.
interview_q: Why does PPO take the min of the clipped and unclipped terms? Model answer: The min makes the objective a pessimistic lower bound. Clipping removes the incentive to move the ratio beyond 1 plus or minus epsilon when that would help the objective, while the unclipped term still penalizes moves that hurt it.
explainer: We start with the policy gradient from last time, but now we want to reuse one batch of samples for several steps.
The ratio on screen compares the new policy's probability to the old one's for every token we sampled.
For a good token, with positive advantage, the objective rises with the ratio until one plus epsilon, then goes flat.
For a bad token, it falls until one minus epsilon, then goes flat, so we never over-correct either way.
Flat means zero gradient, and that is the seatbelt: once a token has moved enough, it stops getting pushed.
For language models, the reward is mostly zero until the last token, with a small KL penalty sprinkled on every step.
And here are the four networks PPO keeps in memory, policy, reference, reward and value, which gets expensive fast.

hook: DPO deletes the reward model and the RL loop. Four lines of algebra turn RLHF into a classification loss.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DPO deletes the reward model and the whole RL loop. Four lines of algebra turn RLHF into a classification loss.

0:15 QUESTION — PPO needs four models and a sampling loop. Zephyr, Tulu and many Llama fine-tunes used DPO instead. Is it an approximation? No. It optimizes the same objective, and today we prove it on the whiteboard.

1:00 INTUITION — The KL-constrained RLHF objective has a closed-form best policy. If you know the best policy, you can read the reward off it. So parameterize the reward by the policy and fit it to preferences directly. [EXPLAINER plays here]
2:30 MATH, STEP 1 — Objective: max_pi E_{x, y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta KL(pi(.|x) || pi_ref(.|x)). Rewrite per prompt as -beta * sum_y pi(y) [log pi(y)/pi_ref(y) - r(y)/beta].

3:30 MATH, STEP 2 — Define Z(x) = sum_y pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) and pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x). The objective becomes -beta KL(pi || pi*) + beta log Z(x). Z does not depend on pi, and KL is zero only at pi = pi*. So pi* is the unique optimum. Say it out loud: the optimal policy is the reference reweighted by exponentiated reward.
5:00 MATH, STEP 3 — Invert: r(x,y) = beta log( pi*(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) + beta log Z(x). Every reward has a policy that is optimal for it, and vice versa, up to the per-prompt constant.

6:00 MATH, STEP 4 — Plug into Bradley-Terry: P(y_w > y_l) = sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)). The beta log Z(x) terms cancel because both answers share the prompt. That cancellation is the whole trick: Z is intractable and we never need it. Replace pi* with pi_theta: L_DPO = -E log sigma( beta log(pi_theta(y_w)/pi_ref(y_w)) - beta log(pi_theta(y_l)/pi_ref(y_l)) ).

7:30 MATH, STEP 5 — Gradient: grad L = -beta E[ sigma(r_hat_l - r_hat_w) (grad log pi_theta(y_w) - grad log pi_theta(y_l)) ], with implicit reward r_hat = beta log(pi_theta/pi_ref). The weight sigma(r_hat_l - r_hat_w) is large when the model currently ranks the pair wrong. Note what beta does: smaller beta lets the policy drift further from the reference.

9:00 CODE — A sympy and numeric sanity check on a toy problem: 5 possible answers, a random r and pi_ref. Compute pi* by formula; then maximize E[r] - beta KL by gradient ascent on logits in PyTorch and show it converges to pi*. Then show log(pi*/pi_ref)*beta recovers r up to a constant.

10:30 RECEIPT — assert_close(pi_from_gradient_ascent, pi_ref * exp(r/beta) / Z, atol=1e-5), and assert that beta*log(pi*/pi_ref) - r is the same constant (beta log Z) for all 5 answers. That is the derivation, verified numerically.
11:30 MEASURE — Plot pi* for beta in {0.1, 1, 10}: small beta collapses onto the argmax reward, large beta stays at the reference.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — DPO is RLHF with the reward model written in terms of the policy, so Z cancels and RL becomes classification. Interview line: the optimal KL-regularized policy is pi_ref times exp(r over beta), normalized, and DPO fits that policy directly to preference pairs.
13:00 NEXT — Next: DPO in code
key_math: pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) exp(r(x,y)/beta) / Z(x); r(x,y) = beta log(pi*(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) + beta log Z(x); L_DPO = -E log sigma( beta log(pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x)) - beta log(pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)) ); grad L = -beta E[ sigma(r_hat_l - r_hat_w)(grad log pi_theta(y_w|x) - grad log pi_theta(y_l|x)) ]
code_task: toy_rlhf(r [K], pi_ref [K], beta) -> pi*: closed form; ascend(r, pi_ref, beta, steps) -> softmax(logits) after maximizing sum pi*r - beta*KL(pi||pi_ref) with torch autograd; check_inverse(pi_star, pi_ref, r, beta) -> beta*log(pi_star/pi_ref) - r (should be constant).
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(ascend(r, pi_ref, beta), pi_ref*torch.exp(r/beta)/(pi_ref*torch.exp(r/beta)).sum(), atol=1e-5); (beta*torch.log(pi_star/pi_ref) - r).std() < 1e-6, i.e. the recovered reward differs from r by a single constant beta*log Z.
gotchas: Forgetting that the reward is only identified up to a per-prompt constant, so 'recovering r' means up to beta log Z; mixing up the KL direction, the RLHF objective uses KL(pi || pi_ref), reverse KL; claiming DPO needs no reference model, it does, pi_ref appears in the loss.
interview_q: Derive why the partition function cancels in DPO. Model answer: Substituting r = beta log(pi*/pi_ref) + beta log Z(x) into Bradley-Terry gives sigma of a reward difference between two responses to the same prompt, so the beta log Z(x) terms are identical and subtract out, leaving only policy and reference log-ratios.
explainer: We begin with the RLHF objective on screen: earn reward, but pay a price for drifting away from the reference model.
This objective has an exact answer, the reference distribution reweighted by the exponential of reward, then normalized.
The normalizer Z sums over every possible answer, so it is impossible to compute, and that is why PPO samples instead.
Now we flip the equation around, writing reward as beta times a log ratio of policies, plus beta log Z.
Feed two answers to the same prompt into Bradley-Terry, and only the difference of their rewards appears.
Both rewards carry the same beta log Z, so it cancels, and the impossible term vanishes from the loss.
What remains is a logistic loss on log ratios, training the policy directly from preference pairs, no reward model, no sampling.

hook: My DPO loss and TRL's DPO loss, same batch, same number to six decimals. Then we train Qwen3 on real preferences.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My DPO loss and Hugging Face TRL's, same batch, same number to six decimals. Then we train Qwen3 on real preference data.

0:15 QUESTION — Last episode was the math. Production DPO has details the paper glosses over: summed vs averaged log probs, the frozen reference, the beta value, and what the logged reward margins mean.
1:00 INTUITION — Four forward passes per pair: policy and reference, on chosen and rejected. Everything else is a logistic loss on two log ratios. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — seq_logp(y) = sum over response tokens of log pi(y_t | x, y_<t), summed, not averaged. Implicit reward r_hat = beta (logp_policy - logp_ref). Loss = -logsigmoid(r_hat_w - r_hat_l). Metrics: reward accuracy = mean(r_hat_w > r_hat_l), margin = mean(r_hat_w - r_hat_l). beta = 0.1 is TRL's default.

4:00 CODE — sequence_logps(model, input_ids [B,T], labels [B,T]) -> [B]: logits[:, :-1], gather at labels[:, 1:], mask -100, sum. dpo_loss(pc, pr, rc, rr, beta) -> loss, chosen_rewards, rejected_rewards. Concatenate chosen and rejected into one [2B, T] batch for one forward. Reference model: a frozen copy in eval mode under torch.no_grad, or precompute its logps once. Start from the SFT checkpoint from M11E03 or Qwen3-0.6B, data trl-lib/ultrafeedback_binarized.

7:30 RECEIPT — Feed the same four logp tensors into TRL DPOTrainer's dpo_loss method (its signature varies by TRL version, read it in the source) and assert_close(my_loss, trl_loss, atol=1e-6). Then the full run: TRL DPOTrainer with DPOConfig(beta=0.1, same LR, same batch) vs my loop for 200 steps, overlay loss and rewards/margins curves.

9:30 MEASURE — Loss, reward accuracy and margin curves, mine vs TRL. Plus a plot of chosen and rejected log probs over training: both often go down, rejected faster. Also reward-model win rate of the DPO model vs the SFT model on 100 held-out prompts, using the reward model from M11E06.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — DPO in code is four forward passes and a logsigmoid, and the receipt is a match to TRL. Interview line: watch the chosen log prob, if it falls a lot the model can get worse at the preferred answer even while the margin improves.
12:00 NEXT — Next: GRPO, derived
key_math: logp(y|x) = sum_{t in response} log pi(y_t | x, y_<t); r_hat(x,y) = beta [ logp_theta(y|x) - logp_ref(y|x) ]; L = -mean log sigma( r_hat(x,y_w) - r_hat(x,y_l) )
code_task: sequence_logps(model, input_ids [2B,T], labels [2B,T]) -> [2B] (sum over unmasked tokens); dpo_loss(policy_chosen [B], policy_rejected [B], ref_chosen [B], ref_rejected [B], beta) -> (loss, chosen_rewards [B], rejected_rewards [B]); dpo_step with a frozen reference model; training loop on ultrafeedback_binarized with Qwen3-0.6B.
receipt: torch.testing.assert_close(my_dpo_loss(pc, pr, rc, rr, beta=0.1), trl_dpo_loss(pc, pr, rc, rr), atol=1e-6) using TRL DPOTrainer's dpo_loss on identical tensors; step-0 full-batch loss = log(2) = 0.6931 when policy == reference (both runs).
gotchas: Averaging log probs over tokens instead of summing, which changes the loss and the effective beta; leaving dropout on in the reference model so its log probs are noisy; letting the prompt tokens into the log-prob sum.
interview_q: At step zero of DPO, what is the loss and why? Model answer: log 2, about 0.693. The policy equals the reference, so both implicit rewards are zero, the margin is zero, and -log sigma(0) = log 2. If you do not see that, your reference or masking is wrong.
explainer: Here is one preference pair, a prompt with a chosen and a rejected answer, ready to go into two models.
The policy and the frozen reference each read both answers, giving us four sequence log probabilities.
Each log probability is a sum over the answer's tokens only, with the prompt masked out exactly like in SFT.
Subtract reference from policy and multiply by beta, and we get the implicit reward for each answer.
The loss is a logistic loss on the gap between the two implicit rewards, which starts at exactly log two.
Our number and TRL's number, computed from the same four tensors, agree to six decimal places on screen.
During training, both answers' log probs often fall, but the rejected one falls faster, and that widening gap is the learning.

hook: GRPO deleted PPO's value network, the biggest model you train, and replaced it with an average. DeepSeek-R1 runs on that idea.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GRPO deleted PPO's value network and replaced it with an average. DeepSeek-R1 was trained on that idea.

0:15 QUESTION — PPO for LLMs keeps a value model as big as the policy, and it is hard to train when reward only arrives at the last token. DeepSeekMath asked: what if the baseline is just how your other answers to the same question scored?
1:00 INTUITION — Ask the same question 8 times. Grade each answer. The answers that beat their siblings get pushed up, the ones below get pushed down. The group is the critic. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH, STEP 1 — Start from PPO: min(rho A, clip(rho, 1-eps, 1+eps) A) with A from GAE and a learned V. Recall from M11E07: any baseline that does not depend on the sampled action keeps the gradient unbiased.

3:30 MATH, STEP 2 — Sample G outputs o_1..o_G for prompt q, rewards r_1..r_G. Outcome advantage for every token of o_i: A_i = (r_i - mean(r)) / std(r). The mean is a Monte Carlo estimate of V(q). Dividing by std rescales per prompt. Note that the mean includes r_i itself, a small bias; leave-one-out (RLOO) removes it.

5:00 MATH, STEP 3 — Objective: J = E[ (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t ( min(rho_{i,t} A_i, clip(rho_{i,t}, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i) - beta D_KL[pi_theta || pi_ref] ) ], with rho_{i,t} = pi_theta(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}) / pi_old(o_{i,t}|q,o_{i,<t}).

6:00 MATH, STEP 4 — KL in the loss, not in the reward. Per-token estimator k3 = pi_ref/pi_theta - log(pi_ref/pi_theta) - 1. It is always non-negative and unbiased for KL(pi_theta || pi_ref) under samples from pi_theta. DeepSeekMath used G = 64, beta = 0.04.
7:00 MATH, STEP 5 — Count the models: policy, reference, and a reward function. For math it is a verifier, not a network. Four models down to two.

7:30 CODE — group_advantages(rewards [N*G]) -> view [N, G], (r - mean) / (std + 1e-4), back to [N*G]. k3_kl(logp, logp_ref) -> [B,T]. grpo_loss(logp_new [B,T], logp_old [B,T], logp_ref [B,T], adv [B], mask [B,T], eps=0.2, beta=0.04): ratio = exp(logp_new - logp_old), per-token clipped term minus beta*k3, mean over tokens per sequence, mean over sequences, negate.

10:00 RECEIPT — Tests. One: advantages sum to zero within each group. Two: a group with all-equal rewards gives zero advantage and zero policy gradient. Three: with logp_new == logp_old and beta = 0, the gradient equals REINFORCE with a group-mean baseline scaled by 1/std, check with autograd. Four: on a toy categorical, the mean of k3 over 1e6 samples equals the exact KL(pi || pi_ref) within 1 percent.
12:00 MEASURE — Memory table for a 1.5B policy: PPO (policy, ref, reward, value + Adam for policy and value) vs GRPO (policy, ref + Adam for policy).

12:45 TAKEAWAY — GRPO is PPO with the critic replaced by the group mean and a KL term in the loss. Interview line: a group where every answer gets the same reward teaches nothing, which is why problem difficulty matters so much in GRPO.
13:15 NEXT — Next: GRPO from scratch on GSM8K
key_math: A_i = (r_i - mean(r_1..r_G)) / std(r_1..r_G); J_GRPO = E[ (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t { min( rho_{i,t} A_i, clip(rho_{i,t}, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_i ) - beta D_KL } ]; D_KL ~ pi_ref/pi_theta - log(pi_ref/pi_theta) - 1
code_task: group_advantages(rewards [N*G], G, eps=1e-4) -> [N*G]; k3_kl(logp [B,T], logp_ref [B,T]) -> [B,T]; grpo_loss(logp_new, logp_old, logp_ref [B,T], adv [B], mask [B,T], clip_eps, beta) -> scalar; pytest with the four tests.
receipt: pytest: group advantages sum to 0 per group (atol 1e-6); zero gradient for a constant-reward group; autograd gradient at rho=1, beta=0 equals the REINFORCE-with-group-baseline gradient; mean k3 over 1e6 samples matches exact KL within 1% (rtol=0.01).
gotchas: Computing std over the whole batch instead of per group, which silently changes the algorithm; dividing by std with no epsilon so all-correct groups produce NaN; using the k1 estimator log(pi/pi_ref) in the loss, which can go negative per token and has much higher variance.
interview_q: Why can GRPO drop the value model? Model answer: For outcome rewards on a prompt, the mean reward of G samples from the current policy is a Monte Carlo estimate of the value of that prompt, so it serves as the baseline. That removes a policy-sized network and its optimizer, roughly halving training memory.
explainer: We start with PPO's four networks on screen, and we are about to delete the biggest helper, the value model.
Instead, we ask one math question eight times and get eight different answers from the same policy.
Each answer is graded right or wrong, and the eight scores form a small group with its own average.
Answers above the group average get a positive advantage, answers below get a negative one, and every token shares it.
If every answer in the group is right, or every answer is wrong, all advantages are zero and that question teaches nothing.
The ratio and the clip are exactly PPO's, and a small KL term keeps us close to the reference model.
Now count the boxes: a policy, a frozen reference and a grading script, which fits on far less memory.

hook: No reward model, no human labels. Just a regex that checks the final number, and GSM8K accuracy climbs on a 1.5B model.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — No reward model. No human labels. A regex that checks the final number, and a 1.5B model gets measurably better at grade-school math.

0:15 QUESTION — DeepSeek-R1-Zero showed RL with verifiable rewards can teach reasoning. CS336 Assignment 5 has you reproduce a small version. Can we do it on one H100 in a few hours, from scratch, and see the curve move?
1:00 INTUITION — Math answers can be checked by code. So the reward is a unit test. Generate, grade, push up the answers that passed. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Reward r = 1 if extracted answer equals ground truth else 0, optionally plus a format reward for the required tags. Group size G = 8, advantages (r - mean)/(std + eps). One rollout batch: N prompts x G samples. On-policy with one gradient step per batch means rho = 1 and the clip is inactive; with several steps per batch the clip matters. Track: mean reward, accuracy on GSM8K test (1,319 problems), mean response length, entropy.

4:30 CODE — Model: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B base, following CS336 A5, with an R1-Zero style prompt that asks for reasoning then an answer inside tags. Rollouts with vLLM: LLM(model, gpu_memory_utilization=0.3), SamplingParams(n=8, temperature=1.0, max_tokens=1024). reward_fn(response, gt) extracts the answer and compares numbers after normalization. Policy update in PyTorch with grpo_loss from M11E11, AdamW lr=1e-6, grad clip 1.0, bf16, gradient checkpointing. After each step, load updated weights into the vLLM engine (see vLLM docs for the weight-loading path in your version, CS336 A5 shows one).

8:30 RECEIPT — Baseline first: zero-shot GSM8K test accuracy of the base model with the same prompt, greedy. Then after training, same eval. Expected: a clear gain, and compare the baseline to the numbers in the CS336 A5 handout as a sanity check. Second receipt: run TRL GRPOTrainer with the same reward function, model and G for the same number of steps and overlay mean reward curves.
10:30 MEASURE — Reward curve, test accuracy every 50 steps, response length curve, and a before/after on one problem. Note the format reward usually saturates first, then accuracy rises.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — RL with verifiable rewards needs a policy, a reference and a grader script. Interview line: most of the work is the reward function and the rollout engine, and the loss is twenty lines. This is the starting point for the reasoning-RL project, P4.
12:30 NEXT — Next: GRPO fixes: Dr. GRPO and DAPO
key_math: r_i = 1[ extract(o_i) == y* ] (+ format bonus); A_i = (r_i - mean_G r) / (std_G r + eps); J = E[ (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t min(rho_{i,t} A_i, clip(rho_{i,t},1-eps,1+eps) A_i) - beta KL ]

receipt: evaluate_gsm8k on the GSM8K test set (1,319 problems, greedy) after training is clearly higher than the same eval on the base model with the identical prompt; baseline is consistent with the CS336 A5 handout; mean-reward curve tracks a TRL GRPOTrainer run with the same reward_fn, model and G.
gotchas: Weights not synced to vLLM after updates, so you keep sampling from the old policy and see no progress; an answer extractor that fails on commas or units ('1,000', '$18') so correct answers score zero; temperature 0 in rollouts so all G samples are identical and every advantage is zero.
interview_q: Your GRPO reward is flat at zero for 100 steps. What is wrong? Model answer: Likely every group is all-wrong, so advantages are zero. Check the extractor and format first, then whether problems are too hard for the base model, then rollout temperature. Seeding with easier problems or a short SFT warmup fixes it.

Out come eight different reasoning traces on screen, each one ending with a number inside answer tags.

vLLM does the fast generation, PyTorch does the gradient step, and after every update the new weights go back into vLLM.
The reward curve on screen climbs, first as the model learns the format, then as it actually gets more answers right.

hook: GRPO's length normalization quietly rewards long wrong answers. Dr. GRPO and DAPO fix that and three other quiet biases.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — GRPO's per-answer length normalization quietly makes long wrong answers cheaper. Two 2025 papers found that and fixed it.

0:15 QUESTION — R1-style training famously shows response length growing. Is that the model learning to think, or a bias in the loss? Dr. GRPO says part of it is the loss. DAPO, which hit 50 on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B, adds four more fixes.

1:00 INTUITION — Dividing by |o_i| spreads a penalty thin over a long answer. So a wrong answer gets less punishment per token if it rambles. And dividing by std makes too-easy and too-hard questions shout louder. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — GRPO per-sequence term: (1/|o_i|) sum_t A_i * grad log pi. With A_i < 0, the per-token penalty is |A_i|/|o_i|, shrinking with length. Dr. GRPO: drop 1/|o_i|, normalize by a constant such as the max generation length, and drop the std, A_i = r_i - mean(r). DAPO: clip-higher, eps_low = 0.2, eps_high = 0.28, so low-probability tokens can grow and entropy does not collapse; dynamic sampling, drop groups with accuracy 0 or 1 and keep sampling until the batch is full; token-level loss, sum over all tokens in the batch divided by total tokens; overlong reward shaping, a soft penalty near the length limit.

6:00 CODE — Add flags to grpo_loss: length_norm in {'seq','token','constant'}, scale_by_std: bool, eps_low, eps_high. Add dynamic_sampling(groups) -> keep groups with 0 < mean reward < 1. Run on the M11E12 setup: three runs, GRPO, Dr. GRPO, GRPO + clip-higher + dynamic sampling, same seed, same steps.

8:30 RECEIPT — Unit test first: with length_norm='seq', a negative-advantage response of length 2L gets half the per-token gradient of one of length L; with 'constant' they get the same. Then cross-check against TRL: GRPOConfig supports loss_type values for grpo, dr_grpo and dapo plus epsilon_high and a reward-scaling option (see TRL docs for exact names in your version); run TRL with the same settings for 100 steps and overlay mean response length.

10:30 MEASURE — The ablation: mean length of incorrect responses vs steps for GRPO vs Dr. GRPO, GSM8K test accuracy at the end, policy entropy with and without clip-higher, and fraction of groups dropped by dynamic sampling. Two seeds minimum; say plainly if the gap is within noise.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — Small normalization choices in the loss change what the model learns, including how long it talks. Interview line: Dr. GRPO removes per-response length and std normalization; DAPO adds clip-higher, dynamic sampling, token-level loss and overlong shaping. This ablation is the template for P4's original contribution.
13:00 NEXT — Next: Reasoning models and test-time compute
key_math: GRPO: (1/G) sum_i (1/|o_i|) sum_t A_i ...; Dr. GRPO: (1/(G*L_max)) sum_i sum_t (r_i - mean r) ...; DAPO: (1/sum_i |o_i|) sum_i sum_t min( rho A, clip(rho, 1-eps_low, 1+eps_high) A ), eps_low=0.2, eps_high=0.28, with groups where all r equal filtered out
code_task: grpo_loss(..., length_norm: str, scale_by_std: bool, eps_low: float, eps_high: float); dynamic_sampling(rewards [N, G]) -> keep mask [N]; three training configs on the M11E12 pipeline; logging of correct vs incorrect response lengths and token entropy.
receipt: pytest: per-token gradient magnitude for a negative-advantage sequence scales as 1/|o_i| under 'seq' and is constant under 'constant'; asymmetric clip leaves gradient non-zero for A>0 at rho in (1.2, 1.28); mean incorrect-response length curve qualitatively matches TRL runs with loss_type set to grpo vs dr_grpo.
gotchas: Comparing runs with different total token budgets, so the 'fix' is just more compute; dynamic sampling that silently shrinks the batch instead of resampling, which changes the effective LR; reading one seed's length curve as a result, length is noisy, run at least two seeds.
interview_q: Why does per-response length normalization in GRPO bias toward longer wrong answers? Model answer: The sequence loss is averaged over its tokens, so a negative advantage is divided across more tokens in a long response, giving each token a smaller penalty. The model learns that wrong answers cost less when they are long.
explainer: Here are two wrong answers to the same question, one short and one three times longer, both with the same negative advantage.
GRPO divides each answer's loss by its length, so the long answer's penalty gets spread thin across many tokens.
Per token, the long wrong answer is punished three times less, and over training the model learns that rambling is safe.
Dr. GRPO removes that division, and it also stops dividing each advantage by the group's standard deviation.
DAPO raises the upper clip from point two to point two eight, so rare but useful tokens are allowed to grow.
It also throws away groups where every answer was right or every answer was wrong, since those carry zero gradient.
Our ablation plots the length of wrong answers over training, one line per variant, so we can see the bias directly.

hook: DeepSeek-R1-Zero went from 15.6 to 71 percent on AIME with pure RL. We measure the cheap version: accuracy versus thinking budget.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-R1-Zero went from 15.6 to 71 percent on AIME 2024 with RL alone. Today we measure what thinking longer buys a small model.

0:15 QUESTION — o1, R1 and Qwen3's thinking mode all spend tokens before answering. Is accuracy really a smooth function of thinking budget, and how does that compare to just sampling more answers and voting?
1:00 INTUITION — Two ways to spend inference compute: think longer in one chain, or think in parallel and vote. Both trade tokens for accuracy, at different rates. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Sequential budget B tokens: truncate thinking at B, force the answer. Parallel: majority vote over k samples, maj@k. pass@k unbiased estimator from n samples with c correct: 1 - C(n-c, k)/C(n, k). Compare at equal total tokens: k * average length vs B. R1 reports 71.0 pass@1 and 86.7 with majority voting for R1-Zero on AIME 2024.

4:30 CODE — Model: Qwen3-1.7B with thinking enabled, served by vLLM. Budget forcing: generate thinking with max_tokens = B and a stop on the end-of-think tag; if the budget is hit, append the end-of-think tag and a short answer cue, then generate the answer. Budgets B in {0 (thinking disabled), 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096}. Parallel: n=16 samples at a fixed small budget, compute maj@k for k in {1,2,4,8,16}. Dataset: MATH-500 or GSM8K test subset of 500.

8:30 RECEIPT — Two checks. My pass@k estimator matches a brute-force combinatorial computation on random (n, c) pairs. And the thinking-disabled vs full-thinking gap on Qwen3-1.7B should point the same direction as the Qwen3 technical report's thinking vs non-thinking numbers; quote the report and compare the direction and rough size.
10:30 MEASURE — The headline plot: accuracy vs total generated tokens on a log x-axis, one curve for sequential budget, one for majority voting. Mark where they cross.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Test-time compute is a real knob, and on small models it saturates. Interview line: R1-Zero showed RL alone can produce long chains of thought, and accuracy scales with tokens spent, but the curve depends on whether you spend them in series or in parallel.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Reward hacking and the KL leash
key_math: pass@k = 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k); maj@k = 1[ mode(answers_1..k) == y* ]; total tokens (parallel) = k * mean_len vs (sequential) = B
code_task: generate_with_budget(llm, prompt, B) -> answer: two-phase vLLM generation with forced end-of-think; pass_at_k(n, c, k) -> float; maj_at_k(answers [k], gt) -> bool; sweep over budgets and k, saving accuracy and mean tokens per config.
receipt: pass_at_k(n, c, k) equals brute-force enumeration over all k-subsets for random n <= 12 (exact match); thinking-off vs thinking-on accuracy gap on Qwen3-1.7B has the same sign and similar size as the Qwen3 technical report's reported thinking vs non-thinking comparison.
gotchas: Truncating thinking and forgetting to close the think tag, so the model keeps thinking inside the answer; comparing budgets without counting answer tokens; computing pass@k as 'any of the first k correct' from one ordering, which is high-variance, use the unbiased estimator.
interview_q: How would you compare scaling test-time compute by longer chains vs more samples? Model answer: Plot accuracy against total generated tokens for both, at the same model and dataset. Longer chains help until the model's useful reasoning length saturates; majority voting keeps helping slowly but needs an answer you can compare. Report both and where they cross.
explainer: Here is one math problem and two ways to spend more compute on it, one long chain or many short chains.
On the left, the model thinks for two hundred fifty six tokens, then a thousand, then four thousand, before answering.
When the budget runs out, we close the thinking block ourselves and ask for the final answer immediately.
On the right, the model answers sixteen times with a short budget, and we take the most common answer.
Now both strategies go on one plot, accuracy against the total number of tokens we paid for.
The sequential curve rises fast, then flattens, because a small model runs out of useful things to think about.
The voting curve climbs slowly but steadily, and where the two lines cross tells us how to spend the next token.

hook: Give an RL policy a reward with one loophole and remove the KL term. Within a few hundred steps it finds the loophole.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Give an RL policy a reward with one loophole, remove the KL term, and it finds the loophole fast. Today we watch it happen.

0:15 QUESTION — Every RLHF objective has a beta times KL term. Labs see reward hacking constantly: verbosity, sycophancy, gaming unit tests. Why does the leash exist, and what does the policy do without it?

1:00 INTUITION — The reward is a proxy. Optimize a proxy hard enough and it stops tracking what you meant. That is Goodhart's law. The KL term says: you may improve, but you must stay recognizable. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — J = E[r] - beta KL(pi || pi_ref). Optimal policy pi* = pi_ref exp(r/beta) / Z from M11E09: beta to zero puts all mass on argmax r, including the exploit. Proxy vs true reward: plot true accuracy against sqrt(KL) as training proceeds; Gao et al. found gold reward first rises then falls as KL grows when optimizing a proxy reward model.

4:30 CODE — Take the M11E12 GSM8K pipeline. Hackable reward: r = 1 if the ground-truth number appears anywhere in the response (a sloppy but realistic grader). True metric: strict last-answer accuracy. Runs: beta = 0, beta = 0.04, beta = 0.1, same seed and steps. Log KL to reference with the k3 estimator, proxy reward, true accuracy, response length, and the count of distinct numbers per response.

8:30 RECEIPT — Show the exploit: in the beta = 0 run, proxy reward approaches 1 while strict accuracy stalls or drops, and distinct-numbers-per-answer climbs. Then fix the grader to strict extraction and show the gap closes. Compare the qualitative shape with Gao et al.'s overoptimization curves.
10:30 MEASURE — Two plots: proxy reward and true accuracy vs steps for each beta; and true accuracy vs sqrt(KL) for each run. Print three example hacked outputs.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — The KL term limits how far the policy can move to exploit a reward, but the real fix is a better reward. Interview line: KL is a leash, not a cure. You detect hacking by tracking a held-out true metric that the optimizer never sees.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Distillation and synthetic data
key_math: J = E_{y~pi}[r(x,y)] - beta KL(pi || pi_ref); pi*_beta = pi_ref exp(r/beta) / Z, beta -> 0 gives argmax r; overoptimization: track R_true vs d = sqrt(KL(pi || pi_ref))
code_task: hackable_reward(response, gt) -> 1 if gt appears anywhere; strict_reward(response, gt) -> 1 if the extracted final answer equals gt; train_grpo(beta in {0, 0.04, 0.1}) reusing M11E12; log proxy, true, kl, length, n_distinct_numbers per step; plot true vs sqrt(KL).
receipt: beta=0 run: proxy reward reaches near 1.0 while strict accuracy is flat or falling and distinct numbers per response rises; beta=0.1 run keeps KL lower and the proxy-true gap smaller; switching to strict_reward removes the gap. Qualitative match to Gao et al. 2022 overoptimization curves.
gotchas: Measuring success with the same reward you optimize, so hacking looks like progress; KL logged with the k1 estimator averaged over few samples, which can look negative, use k3; concluding 'KL fixes hacking' from one seed when it only slows it down.
interview_q: Why is there a KL penalty in RLHF? Model answer: The reward is a learned or approximate proxy that is only reliable near the data distribution. The KL term keeps the policy close to the reference so it cannot drift into regions where the proxy is wrong, which limits reward hacking and preserves fluency.
explainer: Here is our grader with a hole in it: it says correct if the right number shows up anywhere in the answer.
With no KL term, the policy is free to move as far as it wants from the reference model.
A few hundred steps later, answers on screen list every number they can think of, and the grader approves.
The blue line, proxy reward, climbs toward one, while the orange line, true accuracy, goes nowhere.
Turn the KL term back on and the policy is tied to the reference by a leash that gets tighter as beta grows.
Plotted against how far the policy moved, true accuracy rises, peaks, then falls, the classic overoptimization curve.
The leash slows the cheating, but fixing the grader is what actually closes the gap.

hook: DeepSeek's 1.5B distilled model beats far larger models on math. It never ran RL. It copied a stronger model's homework.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B scores 83.9 on MATH-500. It never ran RL. It was fine-tuned on a stronger model's reasoning traces.

0:15 QUESTION — The R1 paper found that for small models, distilling from a big reasoning model beats running RL on the small model directly. Why, and how do you build a distillation dataset that actually helps?

1:00 INTUITION — RL has to discover good reasoning by trial and error. Distillation hands the student worked solutions. Rejection sampling keeps only the solutions that are correct. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Sequence-level distillation is SFT on teacher samples: minimize -E_{y~p_teacher, verified}[log p_student(y|x)], which approximates forward KL(p_teacher || p_student) on the filtered distribution. Logit distillation: per-token KL between teacher and student next-token distributions, needs a shared tokenizer. Rejection sampling: keep y only if verifier(y) = 1. Yield = accepted / generated.

4:30 CODE — Teacher: a stronger open reasoning model served with vLLM, for example Qwen3-8B in thinking mode or DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Generate n=4 traces per GSM8K train problem with max_tokens 2048. Filter with the strict reward from M11E15. Build SFT examples with the chat template, mask the prompt, train Qwen3-0.6B-Base or the M11E12 model with the M11E03 SFT loop, LR 1e-5, 2 epochs.

8:30 RECEIPT — Evaluate on GSM8K test (1,319) with the same prompt and greedy decoding: base, my GRPO model from M11E12, my distilled model. Reference point: R1 reports R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at 28.9 on AIME 2024 and 83.9 on MATH-500, so run that public checkpoint through the same eval script to sanity check the harness.
10:30 MEASURE — Table: accuracy, mean response length, and GPU hours for SFT-distill vs GRPO. Also accuracy vs number of distilled examples (1k, 3k, all) to show the data curve.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — For small models, good traces from a strong teacher are often the cheapest path to reasoning. Interview line: distillation transfers behaviors the teacher found with RL, but it cannot exceed the teacher, and RL on top of distillation is how you push past it.
12:30 NEXT — Next: Number formats

receipt: Running the public DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B checkpoint through my eval script lands near its published level on a matching benchmark (sanity check of the harness); my distilled student beats the base model on GSM8K test, compared against the GRPO model from M11E12 at reported GPU hours.
gotchas: Training on unfiltered teacher traces, so the student learns confident wrong answers; truncated teacher traces (max_tokens hit) slipping into the dataset without a final answer; evaluating with a different prompt or decoding setup than the one used to compare against the GRPO model.
interview_q: When would you distill instead of running RL on a small model? Model answer: When a stronger teacher exists and you can verify its outputs. Distillation is cheaper and more stable, and the R1 paper found distilled small models beat small models trained with RL directly. RL is still needed to exceed the teacher or to optimize things the teacher does not do.
explainer: On screen is a large teacher model and a small student model, side by side, both looking at the same math problem.
The teacher writes four full solutions, long chains of reasoning, each ending with an answer.
Our strict grader checks each answer and throws away the wrong ones, so only verified solutions survive.
The surviving traces become an ordinary supervised fine-tuning set, prompt masked, solution trained, exactly as in episode three.
The student learns to imitate the teacher's reasoning step by step, without ever exploring on its own.
The table compares three students, base, GRPO and distilled, by accuracy and by GPU hours spent.
Distillation copies what the teacher already knows, which is why RL is still needed to go beyond it.
